epub_58.title: Beware of new prime ministers bearing gifts
epub_58.text:
Beware of new prime ministers bearing gifts
Britain
| Enter Andy
Beware of new prime ministers bearing gifts
Andy Burnham avoids telling Britain hard truths
Jul 23rd 2026
Britain’s new prime minister has inherited a country in a funk—and a Labour Party in a slump. On taking office on July 20th, Andy Burnham showed he could tap into the mood of a nation which needs a lift, and a party which needs a fresh start. Speaking in Downing Street, he declared: “Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again.”
Britons are feeling pessimistic about their future. Nearly-two thirds believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, according to polling by Ipsos. This gloomy outlook has persisted since the covid-19 pandemic gave way to a spike in inflation more than four years ago, and Mr Burnham’s four predecessors struggled to shift it. Gathering his cabinet for the first time on July 21st, the prime minister told his team they needed to “take that little bit of pressure off people’s shoulders”.
Mr Burnham is a good communicator; that is why Labour MPs are excited about a change from the stolid Sir Keir Starmer. Alas, his rhetoric has not been matched by a transformative vision for government. Sixteen years after he first tried to become party leader, and a year since he began planning for his new job in earnest, Mr Burnham has hit the ground strolling.
He told his cabinet to be “boldly Labour”, and has railed against 40 years of “neoliberalism” which he claims have devastated parts of Britain, particularly in his home region of the north of England. Mr Burnham has hinted at support for transformative (but probably self-defeating) policies such as wealth taxes, rent controls, the nationalisation of utilities and constitutional reform. None of those, however, made it into his initial policy programme, which is almost entirely short-termist.
Instead, Mr Burnham set out policies of limited ambition designed to fulfil a promise to lead “
a cost-of-living government
”, although wage stagnation, not inflation (which has fallen to 2.6%), is now the biggest constraint on living standards. He cut value-added tax on energy bills from 5% to zero and reintroduced a cap of £2 ($2.67) on bus fares throughout England (other than London, where fares are already cheaper). For businesses, he has promised a discount on the local taxes of certain types of pubs and bars.
The energy announcement was only a modest advance on similar moves by Sir Keir, while the bus cap is a return to an identical policy in place under the previous Conservative government. Both policies will expire within a year of coming into force, and the promised sources of funding look questionable. Previous such small-scale attempts to make life more affordable have not won over voters. Mr Burnham presumably hopes that by setting them out as his very first moves he will convince the public that the long squeeze on their incomes is at last coming to an end.
Although Mr Burnham declared he was “ready”, he has signalled that some of his biggest decisions will be kicked down the road. He has promised to produce a “ten-year plan” sometime in the autumn. This is likely to include his solution to the knotty problem of how to reform social care for the elderly. His biggest policy passion is the devolution of power from Westminster to the English regions, but even there he has provided little detail beyond setting up a “Number 10 North” office in Manchester. Several Starmer-era policies, including the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and a plan to restrict the number of jury trials in order to speed up the courts, are now under review.
As well as boldness on policy, Mr Burnham pledged a politics of unity and an end to Labour’s sniping between factions. That remains to be seen. Mr Burnham immediately fired from the cabinet most of those involved in crafting Sir Keir’s approach to the economy, which (in rhetoric if not always in practice) favoured tech, deregulation and a focus on housebuilding in order to gee up Britain’s sluggish growth.
Rachel Reeves was sacked as chancellor. Peter Kyle, Steve Reed, Liz Kendall and Darren Jones were removed from their posts overseeing, respectively, business, housing, science and the machinery of government. Other casualties included those whose only fault was loyalty to the last prime minister, such as Sir Keir’s deputy, David Lammy. The potential problems with this approach became apparent straight away, as Mr Jones went public with criticism of Mr Burnham’s unfunded spending promises.
By contrast, those Labour bigwigs who had fallen out with the previous regime were rewarded with promotions. Chief among these are the new chancellor, John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary in June after a row over funding, and Wes Streeting, who called for Sir Keir to go and is now in charge of defence. Angela Rayner, Louise Haigh and Lucy Powell—all fired by Sir Keir at some point—are back in senior positions. Ministers who let it be known that they had privately told Sir Keir to quit have either kept their jobs (such as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary) or landed a promotion (such as Ed Miliband, who becomes foreign secretary). Mr Burnham’s commitment to healing old wounds in his party looks shaky.
Mr Healey’s return to the Treasury, where he served as a junior minister in the government of Sir Tony Blair two decades ago, is a welcome signal that Mr Burnham’s assault on economic orthodoxy will go only so far. The new chancellor told the cabinet that “we need to look hard at our own budgets”; given his previous role he is expected to prioritise defence for any new public-spending splurge. Pat McFadden, the flinty work-and-pensions secretary, stays in place, suggesting that efforts to bear down on the welfare bill will continue. Mr Burnham has abolished the standalone department for science and technology, a decision opposed by the tech industry, but made up for it by giving Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, a seat at the cabinet table.
In his first week, the prime minister has preferred quick wins to starting work on the long-term reforms needed to restore Britain to health—and see off the populism of left and right. Though he had friendly phone calls with Donald Trump and other world leaders, his views on foreign policy remain murky. He has said almost nothing about his policy on immigration, the topic which—along with the economy—will decide the next election. He is sending mixed messages on whether he will continue the baleful trend of shifting the tax burden towards higher earners while prioritising pensioners for handouts.
This vagueness leaves Mr Burnham wriggle room to take his government in a more adventurous direction. So far, the early signs are that he is falling short of his grander promises.
■

epub_59.title: Andy Burnham’s first decisions in office reveal a lot about him
epub_59.text:
Andy Burnham’s first decisions in office reveal a lot about him
Britain
| Calorific canapés
Andy Burnham’s first decisions in office reveal a lot about him
They are a worrying taste of things to come
Jul 23rd 2026
In his first days as prime minister, Andy Burnham presented his amuse-bouches to the British public. He announced that VAT, a consumption tax, would be cut on electricity bills from 5% to 0% from October. The cap on most bus fares would be slashed from £3 ($4) to £2 for all of 2027. From April, pubs and clubs in England will get a 20% business-rate cut. Mr Burnham’s portion sizes are meagre: the electricity tax cut will save just £25 per household in this tax year, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a think-tank.
These tasters show Mr Burnham’s strengths. He is a more political animal than Sir Keir Starmer, his predecessor, and understands that tackling the cost of living will be crucial for his success. Unfortunately, he has served up policies that resemble baked Camemberts: they have lots of fatty calories and are liable to cause indigestion later on.
The calorie count is large and growing. Cutting electricity bills costs £850m this tax year alone. Mr Burnham says he will fund it by scrapping Sir Keir’s scheme to introduce digital IDs. But that policy was unfunded, so in reality he will need to find the cash elsewhere. It will be hard to ransack energy budgets, as he has already raided them for £454m to help fund the bus-fare cuts. These early decisions reflect Mr Burnham’s big-spending instincts. If he is not careful, the state’s waistline could balloon.
Nor are Mr Burnham’s offerings nutritious. By
capping bus fares
nationally, he is taking away the agency of mayors to decide how to support their bus networks. That’s the opposite of the devolution dream he ostensibly espouses. He is also blunting price signals.
The electricity tax cut is poorly targeted: richer households will save the most money. And the scrapped digital-ID scheme would in time have made it much easier to use public services. These are ominous signs of a short-termist leader ducking hard decisions.
Mr Burnham says these moves show his promise to “bring back hope”. But the most disgruntled diner is one who gets excited by the menu but disappointed by the food. The best way to tackle the cost of living is to get real wages rising through growth. If Mr Burnham is distracted by £25 giveaways, not even his communication skills will save him.
■

epub_60.title: How Britain’s new prime minister can revive Labour
epub_60.text:
How Britain’s new prime minister can revive Labour
Britain
| Feel the Burn
How Britain’s new prime minister can revive Labour
His supporters are more northern and more Green than Sir Keir’s
Jul 23rd 2026
Labour MPs hope that by picking the former mayor of Greater Manchester to replace Sir Keir Starmer they can clean the slate after
two troubled years in power
. Opinion polls suggest they may be right—at least for now.
Andy Burnham is more popular than Sir Keir (a low bar), but he also has better ratings than the now-departed prime minister had two years ago, when he came to power. Sir Keir squandered the political capital he had at astonishing speed with a series of u-turns and reinventions that voters hated. Though Mr Burnham’s popularity may be equally short-lived, the data suggest that the new Labour leader could build a more enduring electoral base by uniting Britain’s fragmented centre-left voters.
To dig into Mr Burnham’s base of support, The Economist analysed a survey of 5,070 Britons conducted by Stack Data Strategy, a polling firm, between July 7th and 14th. The pollster asked respondents which party they would vote for if an election were held tomorrow. It then repeated the question, asking respondents to consider how they would vote if Mr Burnham were leader of the Labour Party as well as prime minister. The effect was to add 2.1 percentage points to Labour’s vote share—a small but meaningful improvement (see map).
The new prime minister has tied his political identity to the north of England. Northerners have noticed. Across the region Labour’s vote share under Mr Burnham improves by around six points. In his stomping-ground around Manchester the improvement is closer to ten points—not to be sniffed at. Only 26% of seats in Parliament are in the north of England, but over the past decade the region has been rising in political salience. The Economist’s election model suggests that around 45% of the marginal constituencies which Labour needs to win for a parliamentary majority are in the north.
Mr Burnham’s northern roots are also an asset in Britain’s fraught class system. Despite his relatively comfortable upbringing (his father was a BT engineer, his mother a doctor’s receptionist) followed by a degree at Cambridge University, around 46% of Britons say that Mr Burnham is working-class. That compares with only 14% for Sir Keir, the son of a toolmaker, and 18% for the former health secretary (and new defence secretary), Wes Streeting, who was brought up by a single mother in an east London council flat. According to Stack’s data,
replacing Sir Keir with Mr Burnham
would leave Labour’s vote share unchanged among respondents in the most middle-class occupations, while increasing it by 3.6 percentage points among those in the most working-class jobs.
With Mr Burnham’s northern, working-class hue, some commentators mistakenly believe that he is particularly appealing to supporters of the populist-right Reform UK party (many of whom are northern or working-class). In Stack’s polling, however, just 2% of Reform supporters switch to Labour when Mr Burnham is listed as party leader—compared with 4% of Liberal Democrats, 5% of Conservatives and 6% of Green supporters. According to YouGov, another pollster, Mr Burnham has a net favourability rating of +20 points among Green supporters and +21 among Liberal Democrats, compared with a dismal -62 among Reform supporters (see chart). The same voters gave Sir Keir ratings of -47, -14 and -92, respectively.
Faced with this evidence, Mr Burnham might be encouraged to tack to his left, attempting to unite Britain’s broadly left-of-centre bloc in order to defeat Reform. But such an approach brings risks. The first is that left-wing voters tend to be concentrated in relatively few constituencies. Judging by current polls, most Labour MPs could face Reform as the leading challenger in their constituencies. In these contests, switchers from Reform to Labour are in effect worth double.
The second risk is that left-wing voters might not reward Mr Burnham for left-wing policies. There is little evidence that Sir Keir’s most left-leaning policies have won him any friends. His approach—presenting himself as a moderate while pursuing a solidly centre-left agenda—has alienated voters to both his left and right.
In this respect, Mr Burnham begins his time in Downing Street with a head start. Before becoming prime minister, Sir Keir had to contort himself in order to be elected Labour leader by the party’s left-wing membership. As leader of the opposition, he then strained to persuade voters that he was in fact a moderate who had changed the Labour Party. Finally, in government, he had to satisfy the demands of left-wing backbenchers. The whiplash was too much: by May 2026 nearly three-quarters of Britons thought the prime minister was indecisive, according to YouGov. By contrast, voters are still open to finding out what Mr Burnham stands for.
His first electoral test will come sooner than most predecessors’. On July 30th voters in Greater Manchester will elect Mr Burnham’s successor as mayor. Reform won the region with a clear margin in May’s local elections, but polls now suggest that Labour’s candidate—an ally of Mr Burnham—is on course for victory. It would be a good start for Labour.
■

epub_61.title: Tours of British post-war housing are a quiet hit
epub_61.text:
Tours of British post-war housing are a quiet hit
Britain
| Grey expectations
Tours of British post-war housing are a quiet hit
Perambulations of the anti-Instagram kind
Jul 23rd 2026
Langham House Close is the sort of place often passed without a second look. A cluster of low apartment blocks of sandy brick and exposed concrete slabs, it is tucked behind a much grander Georgian mansion which gives it its name. But to the informed visitor, brought by their paper walking-guide to the suburb of Ham in south-west London, it reveals architectural genius. “Note the jutting concrete ‘gargoyles’, inspired by Le Corbusier’s Maison Jaoul,” the guide instructs, of the at-first-glance unremarkable gutter spouts. This was an early work (from 1958) of James Stirling and James Gowan, who would become stars of post-war architecture. Its style became known as “new brutalism” and inspired a generation of British housing.
Finding the poetry in buildings for years dismissed as totalitarian, or plain ugly, is the work of “Perambulations”, a series of walking tours of modernist homes. Their quiet success reflects a wider rehabilitation of ideas about architecture found across the rich world in the decades after the second world war. “Perambulations” started as a pandemic project of Stefi Orazi, a graphic designer, who logged her daily walks around north London’s modernist houses on social media. Set to two sides of paper, a first print run quickly sold out. The series is now on its 30th issue, with more than 40,000 copies sold.
Her typical self-guided tour takes in a couple of dozen properties, mostly in London but also Cambridge, Berlin, Brussels and Paris. Some stops are famous, now found on tea towels and posters. They include the Trellick Tower (in guide number 9), a brutalist monolith in west London designed by Erno Goldfinger. Ian Fleming, an author, so disliked the family home Goldfinger built in Willow Road, Hampstead (guide no 2), that he immortalised the architect as the villain of a James Bond novel.
Others are the early works of future superstars, such as a modest row of mews houses in Kentish Town by Norman Foster and Richard Rogers, who would go on to redraw the skylines of Europe. But the most interesting are the family homes commissioned by middle-class doctors and academics from largely forgotten architects. Ms Orazi’s aim, in part, was to create a historical record. She scours council archives for original plans. “I sometimes think, if I don’t write about them, maybe they never will be [written about].”
Britons enjoy nosying at the homes of their neighbours. But another attraction is the guides’ old-fashioned rigour, an antidote to the age of Instagram. They are printed in two-tone ink with small photographs and dense text. Note, they instruct, how the house numbers are set into the brickwork, and the shape of the decorative lintels. Readers who do not know their pilotis from their paviours soon learn.
Interest in post-war architecture picked up a decade ago as people became worried about the scale of Britain’s current housing shortage, reckons Ms Orazi. The haste to rebuild bombed-out British cities created a legion of opponents; it increasingly looks like a feat worth replicating. For those struggling to raise a deposit for a flat, peering at a family home in north London might produce the same vicarious daydreams as a tour of a country estate.
There is a lot of concrete. But it is not all drab. Take the Alexandra Road estate in Swiss Cottage. Palms and lush climbers spill over the terraced balconies; on a hot July day you might be in Caracas. Or Parkleys, in Ham, built by Eric Lyons’s firm, Span, in the 1950s. The freshly painted olive-green panels, red hung tiling and angular white canopies over the footpaths are as jaunty as if they were made from Lego.
For traditionalists like King Charles, modernist architecture is oppressive, attempting to override the “inner world of humanity” with machine-like rationalism, as he once put it. The architects saw it otherwise: their buildings were stripped of ornament precisely because they prioritised the people inside them. Ms Orazi’s own home in north London, built in the 1970s to designs by Gordon Benson and Alan Forsyth (guide no 3), gives little away on the outside: a long, white building with narrow windows like the slots of a pillbox. But inside the apartments are airy, with split-level floors and huge skylights. “They were designing from the inside out,” she says. “The outside is just a consequence of trying to rationalise the inside.”
There were remarkable opportunities for young architects. Peter Tabori, a Hungarian émigré, was 28 when he was put in charge of Highgate New Town, in north London, which resembles a Tuscan hill town. Not far away is 62 Camden Mews, the family home of Ted Cullinan, an architect (guide no 15). He built it at weekends on a scrap of derelict land with the help of friends; bricks were salvaged from his day job working for Denys Lasdun, the designer of the National Theatre. With heavy black timber frames, angular eaves, a shaded courtyard and entry to the upper floor over something resembling a drawbridge, it is a tranquil pocket of Kyoto on a London backstreet. A smartly positioned letter box drops the Sunday papers into the adults’ bedroom. It sold for more than £900,000 ($1.2m) last year.
Today’s planning system might have suffocated it at birth. Loaded with red tape and vetoes, it rewards safety-firstism, and deters experimentation. It is intended to prevent clunkers; it also weeds out genius. But when cities are free to build, they will often produce delights.
■

epub_62.title: Britons are increasingly tussling over inheritance
epub_62.text:
Britons are increasingly tussling over inheritance
Britain
| Family fortunes
Britons are increasingly tussling over inheritance
More wealth to inherit means more ugly fights
Jul 23rd 2026
When there’s a will, there’s a war. Or so they say in the courts of England and Wales, which are growing busier with fights over the dead’s estates. The number of probate claims listed at the High Court has grown by over 400% over the past decade, according to Solomonic, a legal-analytics company. The first three months of this year saw the highest number filed during any quarter on record. With most disputes over estates settled out of court, this is the tip of the iceberg.
Several factors explain the rise in family fisticuffs. Whereas most of the rest of Europe has “forced heirship” systems, which guarantee spouses and children a fixed share of an estate, in England, Wales and Northern Ireland you can disinherit anyone you like—on whatever grounds you like. Yet at the same time the law in those jurisdictions gives a wide cast of characters—from spouses to stepchildren to financial dependents—a route to challenge a will if they can show they were left without “reasonable financial provision”. As family structures have become both looser and more complex, this has left more people feeling that they might have a right to a slice of the cake.
Demography makes matters worse. Britons are living longer but with conditions (particularly dementia) that can reduce their ability to make sound decisions, prompting more disputes over whether the deceased even had capacity to execute a will. Meanwhile, young people are increasingly reliant on their inheritance to get onto the property ladder: the average age of first-time buyers recently rose to 34 in England, with nearly one in three deposits coming from family gifts, and almost a tenth from inheritance.
The stakes are higher too: the money people stand to inherit—or lose—has never been greater. The government’s tax authority collected a record £8.5bn ($11.5bn, or 0.3% of GDP) in inheritance-tax receipts over the 2025-26 tax year. With thresholds frozen since 2009, and house prices up by more than 70% since then, more estates are being pulled in. Britain’s new prime minister previously suggested he would replace inheritance tax with a progressive “care levy” that everyone would pay, which would make more estates liable.
“There used to be a concern that it was bad form to sue your own relatives. But that is gone,” says Paul Grimwood of Knights, a law firm. He thinks litigiousness has been normalised by TV shows such as “Inheritance Wars”, a Channel 5 documentary series, and tabloid coverage of feuding families. Nearly four in ten respondents to a survey conducted last year by Level Group, a British probate-lending firm, said they would go to court over unexpected or unfair inheritance.
Lawyers expect the uptick in probate disputes to continue. AI-drafted wills are another reason. According to a survey commissioned by the Association of Lifetime Lawyers, an industry training network, 72% of Britons aged 30 to 34 would consider using AI for will-writing. Jessica Medus of Mishcon de Reya, another law firm, says there is a “a genuine access-to-justice argument”; if AI tools prompt more people to think about estate planning, “that is a positive”. But like most litigators, she is mainly worried about the risks. Poorly drafted wills are already a leading cause of disputes; AI chatbots’ tendency towards vague language could produce more.
All this means lawyers dealing with wills, trusts and estates are becoming busier, and more  numerous. Irwin Mitchell, which claims to be one of the largest law firms in the field, has twice as many people working in it as a decade ago. With an estimated £5.5trn expected to pass between generations by 2050, the business is unlikely to slow down. For the families involved, any victory is often pyrrhic. The cruellest inheritance may be a legal bill.
■

epub_63.title: Postcard from the Liz Truss festival of ideas
epub_63.text:
Postcard from the Liz Truss festival of ideas
Britain
| The populist right
Postcard from the Liz Truss festival of ideas
British conservatism is weaker than you think
Jul 23rd 2026
“Disappointing” and “shit” was how some attendees summarised the inaugural CPAC GB conference in Greenwich on July 16th-18th. The event, hosted by Liz Truss, Britain’s shortest-serving prime minister, was inspired by America’s influential Conservative Political Action Conference. Intended as a show of strength for the new right in Britain, it was an advert for its weakness.
Worse than the empty seats were the empty ideas. If CPAC GB was your introduction to British politics, you would come away thinking that Sir Keir Starmer was a communist and that the country is ruled by a sinister coalition of jihadis and “homo-Leninists” funded by George Soros and the Fabian Society (a left-leaning think-tank increasingly singled out as the force shaping Soviet Britain).
In principle CPAC exists to provide a platform for conservatives to share ideas. Britain’s instalment felt more like a Reform UK rally. Its leader, Nigel Farage, who pulled by far the biggest crowd, used his platform to slate both the Conservative Party and Restore Britain, a breakaway far-right party. But in the foyer disgruntled attendees questioned why Tommy Robinson and Restore’s leader, Rupert Lowe, hadn’t been invited.
Britain is often downstream of America, in culture as in politics. But at CPAC GB some of the Yankification fell flat. Daily prayers were sparsely attended. The sponsors were mostly American. Documents seen by the Guardian suggest that the Trump administration intends to allocate $12m ($16m) to British-based conservative groups, including some founded by CPAC GB speakers.
Whether Ms Truss and her fellow-travellers truly believe the paranoid MAGA worldview preached in Greenwich, or whether they just need the money, is hard to say. For all her efforts, the carnival vibe and colourful costumes that define America’s CPAC were missing. In her closing remarks, Ms Truss described how taken she was by the American version of the event. “An experience”, she said, “you will never experience anywhere else.” How right she was.
■

epub_64.title: If Andy Burnham is going to achieve big things, he has to act now
epub_64.text:
If Andy Burnham is going to achieve big things, he has to act now
Britain
| Bagehot
If Andy Burnham is going to achieve big things, he has to act now
Why the first 100 days really matter
Jul 23rd 2026
Changing prime minister has become an all too familiar ceremony. On July 20th Sir Keir Starmer bade farewell and zipped from Downing Street to Buckingham Palace, with helicopters hovering above. Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, followed in reverse, heading from Buckingham Palace to Downing Street, where friends, family, allies and apparatchiks listened to his hopes for Britain.
Then began the next stage: picking over every word. What did Mr Burnham mean when he called his government a “circuit-breaker”? Was his target to eliminate rough sleeping feasible? And most important: what will Mr Burnham do in his first 100 days?
At this point, the chuntering starts. Why judge a government that will run the country for years after only 100 days? Forget the first days, what about the next ten years? What better symbol of the adhd-addled media environment that makes governing impossible? But whereas most media conventions can be dismissed, the first-100-days meme cannot. It reflects a fundamental truth of British politics. The most consequential government actions happen almost immediately or not at all.
Take Sir Tony Blair. Practically all New Labour’s lasting achievements happened within days of taking power. Bank of England independence, which is now the backbone of British economic policy, came on day five. A plan to give Scotland and Wales their own parliaments, on day 14. By the end of the first month, the national minimum wage was in progress. After eight weeks, what became the Human Rights Act was outlined. To round off this busy first 100 days, plans for a London mayor were unveiled.
What about the next dozen years? Oh, they did this and that. Public services improved; waiting lists fell, eventually. Schools were rebuilt; the public realm was renewed. But this was temporary, as a trip down any high street or a visit to hospital today will show. New Labour’s achievements faded away and Sir Tony, the most successful prime minister of the past 30 years, spent two decades kicking himself for not doing more sooner.
And so it was for the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government led by David Cameron that took power in 2010. Austerity was put in train at once; the government announced it would crank vat to its current level of 20% after a little over a month. The triple lock, which guarantees that the state pension must rise by the rate of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%, came on the 42nd day of the Cameron era. A good 16 years on, it is still there, a symbol of the long-term unseriousness of British policy, since it will eventually lead to the heat-death of the fiscal universe unless someone tweaks it.
By 2014 the legislative cupboard was almost bare. Critics called it a zombie parliament. Whips desperately emailed MPs for ideas for debates. (Perhaps food security? What about foreign lorries?) When Mr (now Lord) Cameron won a majority in the 2015 election, he set Brexit in train almost immediately. He produced the referendum bill on the eu on day 21, sealing his government’s fate.
Likewise, Theresa May took her biggest decisions within weeks of winning power. At her first Conservative Party conference as leader, Mrs (now Lady) May set Britain on a path to a hard Brexit. Her place in history was secured by day 82. It took Boris Johnson a bit longer to rejig Britain’s relationship with Europe: he reached a deal with the eu on day 86, which was one half of his legacy. The other half was a boom in immigration. When did Mr Johnson ditch the Conservative Party’s long-held pledge to cut immigration to “tens of thousands”? Day one.
Most governments take up to 100 days or so to shape a country. Liz Truss managed it in half that. She pledged energy subsidies roughly equivalent to the annual British defence budget. When a ragbag of sweeping tax cuts were thrown in, markets moved, Tory mps followed and Ms Truss was gone. Unpicking that budget was Rishi Sunak’s job, which he did in the first few weeks. Grill veterans of the Sunak era about their achievements and at the top comes the Windsor Framework, which restored relations between the eu and Britain to normalcy, and dominated the start of Mr Sunak’s tenure. Little else matters from Mr Sunak’s stint.
What happens when a government fails to sprint at the start? Ask drinkers at The Grafton, a pub in north London, which on July 20th hosted relieved and humiliated members of Sir Keir’s team, who toasted their freedom from the burdens of government barely two years after a landslide victory.
Of all the sins of Sir Keir’s time in office, it was the start that proved mortal. In the first 100 days of Sir Keir’s tenure there was a great vacuum where a government should be. In the time that other governments had begun upending Britain’s constitution or ripping through the country’s fiscal position or taking Britain out of Europe, Sir Keir cut winter-fuel payments to pensioners, embroiled himself in a scandal about the number of freebies he accepted and sacked his chief of staff. After barely two months in power, prescient obituaries of “two-year Keir” were written, even if they felt absurd at the time.
First impressions are usually correct. Governments do not change much in office. Errors compound and events scar them, but their basic instincts and flaws remain the same. To the extent that prime ministers control their destiny at all, they control their first few months. And so the most significant period of Mr Burnham’s government has already begun. A strategy for the next decade is coming, says Mr Burnham, but in the autumn. Judging by his predecessors, it could well be too late. They had already been assigned their place in history by that point. If Mr Burnham has a plan, Britain needs to hear it soon, or it never will.
